title: More internet, less corruption? Not always

voiceover.text: Put a country online, and corruption has nowhere to hide. That's the idea, anyway.
And in twenty twelve, the data agreed. The more people online, the cleaner the country looked.
Only six countries had more than ninety percent of people online. All six were among the cleanest in the world.
Twelve years later, the world got online. Average internet use nearly doubled.
So corruption scores should have improved too. They barely moved.
So, does the internet make a country cleaner?
Not always. Today, fifty countries are past ninety percent online. Their scores run from ninety, all the way down to twenty-two.
Russia is about as online as the U.S. The U.S. scores sixty-five. Russia scores twenty-two.
Year after year, the link between the two has been getting weaker.
Thailand went from a quarter of people online to over ninety percent. Its score went down, from thirty-seven to thirty-four.
Japan has fewer people online, and scores seventy-one.
And it works the other way too. Rwanda has a third of people online, and still outscores Thailand and China.
Getting online opens the door. It doesn't decide who walks through it.
We joined two open datasets on Querious: the World Bank's internet data, and Transparency International's index.
Find your own country, then download the result, or connect it to your own AI and tools.
The data is open. The question is yours.
